title: The way things used to be

fn.en: Talk about how things used to be and are no longer, and talk about the news.

items.q: A volcano does this when it explodes: it ___s.

sub.en: Look at the pairs. Which one says “and it isn’t true any more”?

items.q: I ___ smoke, but I gave up in 2015.
items.why: used to = it was true repeatedly or for a long time, and it is NOT true now. The Past Simple just says it happened.

items.q: I ___ smoking in 2015. (one action, one moment)
I ___ like olives, but now I do.
items.why: After didn’t, the form is use to — no d. The past is already in didn’t.

use: …is the second disaster to affect the region.
tts: The forest fire in the woods of the northern provinces is the second natural disaster to affect the region after last June’s floods.
The area also has very high unemployment, with around forty per cent of under-thirty-year-olds out of work.
Yesterday we heard that a multinational company has decided not to build a new factory here. People had hoped this would create jobs in the region.
When they heard the news, several hundred people gathered outside the town hall.

items.q: What is the news story?
What happened in the region last June?
How many under-thirties are out of work?
What did the company decide?
What had people hoped?
What did people do when they heard?

acts.title: How we used to find out
text: My grandfather used to get the news once a day, at nine in the evening, from a radio he did not own — it belonged to the whole street and it lived in the shop.

He didn’t use to know anything before that hour, and he says nobody minded. When something enormous happened, it reached the village late, sometimes by two days, and by then it had already been decided what it meant.

He gave up listening to the news in 2011, at the age of seventy-eight. He says it changed: it used to be a report of what had happened, and now it is a report of what is happening, which is a different thing and much harder to be told at nine in the evening.
He still reads one newspaper a week. If he had a phone, he says, he would read nothing at all, because he has watched everybody else stop reading.
I told him this was a bit unfair. He said, correctly, that I was reading my phone at the time.

items.s: His grandfather used to get the news once a day.
News used to reach the village immediately.
He gave up listening to the news in 2011.
He says the news has stayed the same.
He still reads a newspaper every week.

write.q: Describe how your life or your country used to be: 6 sentences. Use used to three times, didn’t use to once, one Past Simple for a single finished event, and one question with Did you use to…?
write.model: I used to walk to school past a market that isn’t there any more. My mother used to buy bread from the same woman for eleven years, and I didn’t use to understand why that mattered. The market closed in 2013 and the woman moved to another district. We used to see her twice a year after that, and then we stopped. Now there is a supermarket and the bread is worse and cheaper. Did you use to have a shop like that where you grew up?

speak.q: Answer out loud: What did you use to do as a child that you don’t do now? What didn’t you use to like? How did people use to get the news where you live?
speak.model: I used to walk everywhere and I used to read paper books. I didn’t use to like coffee at all. My grandparents used to get the news once a day, from the radio in the shop.
